newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnians head to controversial post-war poll.
newsitem.headline: Bosnians head to controversial post-war poll.

text.p: Bosnia votes on Saturday in elections which could kill it off as a multi-ethnic state or provide a lifeline towards a possible stable democracy.

When Bosnians last voted in 1990, ethnic nationalist parties triumphed and set the stage for Europe's worst war for half a century. This time some 55,000 mainly NATO troops are on hand to prevent history repeating itself.
The elections were set up by the Dayton peace accords, thrashed out last November to end 43 months of war.
Critics still say they are a mistake which could kill forever hopes of a reunified, multi-ethnic state, cement partition and legitimise the results of conquest, ethnic cleansing and genocide.

International organisers admit the polls are far from "free and fair" as stipulated by Dayton. But they say they are essential if Serbs, Moslems, and Croats are to start the process of building common institutions laid out in the Dayton accords.

Almost three million voters will elect a collective three- man presidency and national parliament, a president for the Serb Republic (RS), separate assemblies for the RS and Moslem-Croat Federation, and cantonal administrations.

There is little doubt about the outcome. The wartime leaders and their parties dominate their respective fiefdoms and have failed to respect Dayton's own terms for freedom of movement, association and expression.
The Bosnian Serb Democratic Party (SDS) holds unchallenged sway in the 49 percent of the country it carved out for itself through conquest, killings and expulsions.

It sees the poll as legitimising its rule and bringing its stated goal of a separate state ever closer. It already treats as a border the administrative boundary with a Moslem-Croat Federation, an entity currently existing mainly on paper.

Hardline Bosnian Croats of the Croatian Democratic Union party want union with Croatia. In the southwestern town of Mostar, Moslems to the east and Croats to the west of the river Neretva still eye each other nervously amid little sign of reconciliation.

The Croatian flag fluttered on Friday over Jajce, an open proclamation of its Croat masters' real allegiance. Moslems were once the town's biggest community, but few have dared return since it was captured from the Serbs exactly one year ago.
Those who return to vote will come in buses and hastily leave afterwards.

The ruling Moslem Party of Democratic Action (SDA) makes little secret that its support for Dayton arises from the fact that, supported by the largest single ethnic group, it would dominate any reconstituted state.
Independent analysts say it has become increasingly narrow and intolerant, only allowing opposition which poses no threat.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), which is running the election, has lowered its sights as reports of breaches of the rules have flooded into its Sarajevo headquarters. The aim now is a "democratic and effective" poll.
President Bill Clinton has sent his mercurial envoy Richard Holbrooke, the architect of Dayton, to observe the polls and promised continued U.S. support for the peace process.

"These elections are a key step on the long, difficult path to a lasting peace in Bosnia -- a path we are determined to walk alongside the Bosnian people in the days ahead," Clinton said in a statement on Thursday.
Arriving at Sarajevo airport, Holbrooke said it was important to have elections this year even if they were imperfect, and again stressed that secession was not an option.

Holbrooke said the poll would allow the creation of a presidency, national assembly, constitutional court, central bank and single currency, and allow the implementation of other aspects of Dayton which have not yet been carried out.
The elections are a logistics nightmare.

Some 4,600 polling stations are manned by 35,000 election workers, almost 1,000 foreign supervisors, and hundreds of independent monitors overseeing a total of some 28,000 candidates in 50 political parties.
Thousands of refugees outside Bosnia have already voted.
Early on Friday, selected polling stations opened on both sides of the ethnic divide to allow soldiers and police on duty on Saturday to vote early.
One of them, a Serb soldier voting in the town of Stricici, was not optimistic, saying: "I'm afraid this will turn into something totally different from what the world wants."
